children.text: Mr Darcy's first glimpse of Elizabeth Bennett. It becomes very clear that he's attracted to her just from that quick glance, and then he studiously avoids eye contact.

Mr Darcy's attraction to Elizabeth is undeniable. Every time she enters the room, all of his attention is immediately focused on her. She feels rather uncomfortable from his attention, because she doesn't understand what it means.

This scene is more an example of the barrier than of Mr Darcys attraction. In this scene, he comes across as rather arrogant and demanding. The closes he gets to showing a sign of his attraction to Elizabeth is at the end, where he suggests an accomplished woman should open her mind by reading, and Elizabeth closes her book immediately.

Mr Darcy helping Elizabeth into the carriage is one of the most recognisable scenes from the film. It is where his attraction to Elizabeth becomes the most obvious. The way he flexes his hand, like he's trying to remember what it felt like to hold her hand.

This scene is a callback to the first ball Elizabeth and Mr Darcy both attended, where she asked if he danced and he said "not if I can help it." His decision to ask her to dance explores the attraction he feels for her in a very subtle way. It makes it clear that though he dislikes dancing, he would happily dance with her. His lack of expression could be interpreted as dismissive formality (which is likely how Elizabeth sees it) but it could also be interpreted as nerves.

Elizabeth is completely shocked at this turn of events, because she is still acting under the assumption that he doesn't like her. He has not done the best job of showing her his interest. His decision to ask Elizabeth to dance is his announcement of his feelings and regard for her, but she doesn't pick up on that.
